 Americans Have Forgotten Money Sitting With Their State Treasurer. Here’s How Retirees Are Finding It.
 By Austin Smith 
 Published November 19, 2026, 10:12am ET · 3 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Dormant accounts, uncashed checks, deposits and insurance proceeds get turned over to states, but owners keep their rights, and retirees with long address histories or inherited estates are especially likely to have claims.
 Clark Howard advises searching MissingMoney.com first, then unclaimed.org, covering every state, former names and deceased parents' names before filing claims on official state sites.
 Searching and claiming costs nothing through official programs, so avoid finders demanding upfront payment; returned principal isn't taxable income, though interest above $10 triggers a 1099-INT.

 When a checking account goes dormant, a final paycheck never gets cashed or a utility deposit never gets refunded, the business holding that money eventually turns it over to the state. New Jersey’s Unclaimed Property Administration describes how it works: when property reaches the abandonment period set by state law with no activity, the holder turns it over to the state [ 1 ] , and the owner "never relinquishes ownership." The money stays in trust until someone files a valid claim. Dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, utility deposits, insurance proceeds and safe deposit box contents all land in this category.
 Most finds are small. On his June 4, 2018 podcast, Clark Howard told listeners that claims "usually will be in the hundreds of dollars most of the time," with occasional larger amounts. In a June 3, 2026 episode, he noted that some state databases show only a range, such as less than $100, less than $500 or less than $10,000.
 Why Retirees Are Most Likely to Have Money Waiting
 A long life usually means a long list of addresses. Each move can leave something behind: an apartment security deposit, a utility refund check sent to the old house, or a last paycheck from an employer that later merged or shut down. Accounts closed decades ago can leave small credit balances that nobody ever collects.
 Families add more layers. If your parents have died and you are an heir, money held in their names may now be yours to claim. Insurance proceeds and safe deposit box contents often go unclaimed because the people who knew about them are gone.
 How to Search Every State You Have Lived In
 Start at MissingMoney.com . The National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA) sponsors this free website, which searches the databases of participating states at once.
 Check holdout states directly. A few states do not participate. Unclaimed.org links to each state’s official unclaimed property program. Howard’s order: "MissingMoney.com is the first search, unclaimed.org is the second."
 Search every state on your address history, including places you lived only briefly.
 Search former names, including maiden names and common misspellings.
 Search deceased parents’ names if you are an heir. Expect the state to ask for estate paperwork.
 File the claim on the state’s official site and send the identity and address documents it asks for.
 Fees, Taxes and Scams to Know Before You Claim
 Cost: NAUPA states that "there is no fee to search for and claim your unclaimed property" when you go through the official state program. Third-party "finders" are in most cases legal, but they take a cut for work you can do yourself in an afternoon. Steer clear of anyone who asks for money upfront. Scammers also pose as government officials: impersonation scams were among the complaints in the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s 2025 annual report. A real state program never needs your bank login.
 Taxes: New Jersey’s administrators say returned property already belongs to you [ 1 ] , so the principal is not counted as income. The state does pay interest while it holds the money, and if that interest tops $10 [ 1 ] , you will get a 1099-INT in January. Earnings on the property, such as stock dividends, may also be taxable. Rules vary by state, so bring any tax forms to your tax preparer.
 This suits anyone who has moved, changed jobs or settled a parent’s estate. A search costs nothing but time. The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index sits at 48.1 [ 2 ] in September 2026, a level the survey’s guide calls recessionary, and even a few hundred dollars can help a budget built on fixed income.
 Run Your Search This Week
 Write down every state you have lived in, every name you have used and the full names of any parents whose estates you inherited. Then run each one through MissingMoney.com and the official state sites linked at unclaimed.org. If something turns up, file the claim directly with the state, where it costs nothing.
